above_gcse.text: Payback time = extra cost of the efficient appliance ÷ yearly saving on energy bills.
above_gcse.why: Payback time is not in spec 4.1.2.2. The spec requires only the two efficiency equations, use of decimals and percentages, and (HT) ways to increase efficiency. The lesson also gives payback a checkpoint, and keyPoints[3].tutor_note tells students to 'Know both formulas'. This presents payback as required content, which it is not.

above_gcse.text: Energy efficiency labels: UK and EU appliances carry an A–G energy label. A is the most efficient, and G is the least.
above_gcse.why: Energy labels are not part of the specification section. They also appear in revisionCardBullets as if they were content to learn.

above_gcse.text: Comparing devices is a common exam question. Know rough efficiency values for LEDs and filament bulbs. Know them for electric and petrol vehicles too.
above_gcse.why: The spec does not require students to recall efficiency values for particular devices. It says 'Students may be required to calculate or use efficiency values'. Telling students to memorise device values, including electric vehicles, solar panels and the human body, goes beyond the spec. Several of the values given are also inaccurate (see factual_errors).

above_gcse.text: The human body: about 25% efficient at turning chemical energy (food) into mechanical energy.
above_gcse.why: Human body efficiency is not in the spec. It also brings in 'mechanical energy', which is not one of the spec's energy stores.

above_gcse.text: Electric vehicles: ~85–90% efficient. The motor is very efficient, and regenerative braking recovers more energy.
above_gcse.why: Electric vehicle efficiency and regenerative braking are not required by 4.1.2.2. Regenerative braking is also listed in revisionCardBullets as a way to improve efficiency, but the spec does not name it.

factual_errors.text: Imagine you pay for 100 units of electricity and only get 25 units of useful motion. That is a petrol car engine.
factual_errors.correction: A petrol engine is supplied with chemical energy from fuel, not electricity. The example should say something like '100 units of energy from fuel'.

factual_errors.text: a petrol car engine has an input power of 100 kW. It gives out 25 kW of kinetic energy
factual_errors.correction: Kilowatts measure power, not energy. It should say 'a useful power output of 25 kW'. This matches the spec's 'efficiency = useful power output / total power input'.
Fluorescent tubes transfer only about 20–30% of their electrical input as visible light. A figure of 70–80% is far too high. The same error appears as '~75% (0.75)' in tables[0].

Typical LED lamps transfer roughly 30–50% of their electrical input as light. They are far better than filament bulbs (about 5%), but ~90% overstates them. The same figure is repeated in intro, tables[0], checkpoints['1'] and revisionCardBullets.

factual_errors.text: No real machine is 100% efficient. Some energy is always wasted, usually as thermal energy (heat) or sound.
factual_errors.correction: Efficiency depends on which output counts as useful. An electric heater, where the thermal output is the useful output, is close to 100% efficient. Most devices waste some energy, but the blanket statement is not true for every device.
Light that is reflected stays as light (radiation). It is not transferred to a thermal store. Only absorbed light that is not converted to electricity heats the panel.

wrong_terms.text: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy
wrong_terms.spec_term: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer

wrong_terms.text: efficiency = useful output power (W) ÷ total input power (W)
wrong_terms.spec_term: efficiency = useful power output / total power input

wrong_terms.text: about 25% efficient at turning chemical energy (food) into mechanical energy
wrong_terms.spec_term: useful output energy transfer (the spec does not use 'mechanical energy')

checkpoint_mismatch.why: The checkpoint depends on knowing that LEDs are about 90% efficient and filament bulbs about 5% ('~90% vs ~5%'). Those values are taught in keyPoints[2] 'Comparing efficiencies of different devices', not in keyPoints[1]. KeyPoints[1] only mentions an LED at 0.9 and never mentions filament bulbs. So the checkpoint does not test the calculation key point it sits with, and keyPoints[2] has no checkpoint of its own.
